concept.name: FX forward
concept.definition: An over-the-counter contract to exchange one currency for another at a rate fixed today for settlement on a specific future date beyond the spot value date. Outright forwards are used mainly to hedge future currency payments and receipts, and accounted for 15% of global OTC FX turnover in April 2022.
concept.intuition: An FX forward locks in today the exchange rate for a currency trade you will make weeks or months from now.
concept.mechanics: The forward rate equals the spot rate adjusted by forward points reflecting the interest rate differential between the two currencies over the contract tenor (covered interest parity). A single outright forward involves one exchange of principals at maturity; non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) settle only the net value difference in a convertible currency. Unlike futures, forwards are bilateral OTC contracts and carry counterparty risk.
concept.formula: F = S x (1 + r_q x T) / (1 + r_b x T), where F = forward rate, S = spot rate (quote per base), r_q = quote-currency interest rate, r_b = base-currency interest rate, T = tenor in years under the applicable day-count convention.
concept.failure_modes: Forward rates are a no-arbitrage pricing output, not forecasts of future spot rates; since 2008 persistent cross-currency basis deviations mean forward pricing also embeds balance-sheet costs. Bilateral forwards carry counterparty credit risk absent in centrally cleared instruments.
concept.misconceptions: A forward rate is not the market's expected future exchange rate; it is mechanically derived from the spot rate and money-market rates.
concept.example: A US importer owing EUR 10 million in six months buys a 6-month EUR/USD forward at 1.0920; whatever the spot rate is at maturity, the euros cost exactly USD 10.92 million.
